k449: Sarandë asks €2,000–2,500/m² for new build within a kilometre of the sea, and its 430 short-term listings run at about 41% occupancy. The strip matters more than the city figure: the promenade reaches €3,000–3,500/m², the centre is €1,600–1,800 turnkey, and Ksamil is €1,800–3,000. Foreign demand has fallen two years running while prices rose, and that gap is the thing to understand before buying here.

k460: The 2025 Shëngjin–Velipoja road cut 66 km to under 15, and the town sells at €1,100–2,000/m² to mostly Kosovar and diaspora buyers. The mass segment sits at €1,100–1,500; the top of the band goes to premium residences on the front. A flat here takes about three to three and a half months to sell, and the state reference price is 49,200 lek/m².

k465: Shkodër publishes no single average, deliberately: prime central new build runs €1,700–1,900/m², while peripheral and older stock sits at €800–1,200. New-build prices roughly doubled in four to five years, and the driver was a shortage of building permits rather than foreign demand — which is why the two halves of this market moved so differently.

One caution on growth — the Bank of Albania's index shows the market flat half on half through the second half of 2025, after rising 56% the year before, so claims built on listing prices deserve scepticism.

k487: Vlora averaged €2,400/m² in 2025, up 25% year on year — with Tirana, the fastest growth in Europe. Inside that the spread is wide: the Lungomare promenade asks €2,500–3,500/m² and has doubled since 2022, while the centre and boulevard still serve local buyers from €800/m². One thing to weigh before buying — the airport still had no flights as of summer 2026, and the expectation that it will is already in the prices.

k498: 21 Dhjetori is a transit district and makes no secret of it: traffic runs through it all day, which is exactly why it costs €1,800–2,200/m² new and €1,400–1,800/m² resale instead of Blloku money, despite being a short walk away. That trade suits one buyer in particular — a landlord letting to young professionals who want the centre within walking distance and will accept the noise for a lower rent. Anyone buying to live in should visit at rush hour before deciding. The reference rate, 114,300–159,100 lek/m², reflects an area that is central in access rather than in character.
k499: The loudest crossroads in Tirana, and a ten-minute walk from Blloku.
k500: Central access at a discount for the noise: €1,800–2,200/m² new, €1,400–1,800/m² resale, minutes from Blloku.

k505: Ali Demi is one of the older residential quarters, anchored now by the Continental Hospital and the Bektashi World Centre, and it trades on distance rather than glamour: €1,400–1,800/m² for new builds and €1,100–1,500/m² for resale puts the centre within a short ride for well under central money. Gentrification here is slow and visible, building by building rather than block by block. Its official reference rate, 97,200–102,800 lek/m², is one of the tightest bands in Tirana, which tells you the area is homogeneous — you are unlikely to overpay by picking the wrong street.
k506: Old Tirana within reach of the centre, at a price the centre stopped offering years ago.
k507: Older Tirana minutes from the centre: €1,400–1,800/m² new, €1,100–1,500/m² resale, and one of the city’s tightest reference bands.

k512: Astir and Unaza e Re are where families priced out of the centre have been going, and where developers followed them: new builds start around €1,400/m², up from €1,200–1,300 in 2024, with resale at €900–1,200/m² and a one-bedroom letting for €200–350 a month. The area carries Tirana’s clearest oversupply risk — if demand softens, this is where the 10–15% discounts appear first. Its upside is tied to two public projects, the ring road completion and the railway, both of which run on state timelines. We publish no official reference price here: the street directory does not resolve Astir to an administrative unit, and guessing one would dress a gap up as a fact.
k513: The largest new-build front in the south-west — and the city’s clearest oversupply risk.

k520: Blloku (Ish-Blloku) is the former closed party quarter, today the epicentre of Tirana’s bars, boutiques and offices. It is the most prestigious and most walkable central district, popular with the local elite, buy-to-let investors and foreign buyers. As of 2026, new builds trade around €3,000–5,500/m² and resale around €2,500–3,500/m², among the highest in the city. The upside is prestige, safety and liquidity; the trade-offs are noise, traffic and tight parking. Blloku suits buyers who value capital preservation and status over maximum rental yield.
k523: Blloku is Tirana's most vibrant district.
k525: Blloku, Tirana: New builds €3,000–5,500/m², resale €2,500–3,500/m², a 1+1 rents for €500–700/month. Sourced asking prices, 2026-H1.
k528: The New Boulevard is where Tirana is being rebuilt rather than filled in: a master plan covering roughly a fifth of the city, the mayor’s office and the courts moving in, and a Qatari-funded square. First-line asking prices start around €2,700/m² while the second line sits near €1,900/m² — and that second line rose 36% in a year, the fastest move in Tirana. What you are buying is the plan, not the neighbourhood as it stands today, so the honest horizon is three to seven years and the honest risk is that state construction runs late. The reference rate straddles two administrative units, 93,600–163,600 lek/m², which is another way of saying the area is not yet one settled place.
k529: The city’s biggest construction bet: a master plan for a fifth of Tirana, with the price already reflecting it.
k530: Tirana’s fastest-rising area and its longest horizon: €2,700/m² first line, €1,900/m² second, +36% in a year.

k535: Fresku and Linzë climb the eastern slope toward Mount Dajti, close enough to the Dajti Express cable car and Bunk’Art 1 to make weekends easy and far enough up that the air is noticeably better than downtown. Prices sit at €1,400–1,500/m², up 16–27% from €1,100–1,200 in 2024, and the driver is specific: the new road connecting the area to the Grand Ring. That same road is the risk, because the district depends on it almost entirely — one route in, one route out. The official reference rate here is 75,500 lek/m², among the lowest inside greater Tirana, which is the trade you make for the hillside.
k537: The slope up to Dajti, cleaner air than the centre, and one road in and out.
k539: The Dajti hillside at €1,400–1,500/m², up 16–27% since 2024 — and dependent on a single road.

k543: Dhërmi is a boutique resort market rather than a mass one, held up by festivals like Kala and ION and the UK audience they bring. New build lists around €3,000/m², luxury projects run €1,500–2,500 and first line reaches €3,500, while stone villas start near €167,000 at about €2,000/m². We deliberately publish no state reference price for Dhërmi. The sources give two: 186,400 lek/m² as a town rate and 58,000 as a Himarë village rate — a 3.2× disagreement that is a dispute about how the place is classified, not a difference between schedule editions. Quoting either as fact would be misleading, so the market figures stand alone until the classification is settled.
k544: The Riviera’s festival address, and the widest official-versus-market gap in Albania.

k550: Don Bosko has the things people actually use daily — cafés, markets, a park, the German school — without the price of a central postcode. New builds ask €1,500–2,000/m² and resale €1,200–1,600/m²; a one-bedroom rents for €250–400 a month, a two-bedroom for €400–600, which lands roughly €100–300 below the equivalent in Blloku. The trade is density: this is a tightly built quarter and it is getting tighter as it gentrifies. For a landlord chasing yield rather than a prestige address, that gap between price and rent is the whole argument.
k551: Cafés, markets and a park, at a hundred to three hundred euros a month below Blloku rents.
